questions.q: Which background process is responsible for cleaning up after a failed user process, per this lesson?
options: PMON
DBWn
CKPT
LGWR
questions.explain: PMON (Process Monitor) releases locks and rolls back incomplete transactions left behind by a failed process.

questions.q: Which process writes modified ('dirty') buffers from the buffer cache out to the datafiles on disk?
options: DBWn
SMON
PMON
CKPT
questions.explain: DBWn (Database Writer) writes dirty buffers to the datafiles; there can be more than one on heavy-write systems.

questions.q: What is the role of LGWR, per this lesson?
options: It writes entries from the redo log buffer in memory out to the online redo log files on disk
It performs instance recovery after a crash
It caches parsed SQL statements and execution plans
It allocates private memory for each server process
questions.explain: LGWR flushes redo log buffer entries to the online redo log files, making committed changes durable.

questions.q: What are the main components of the SGA, per this lesson?
options: The database buffer cache, the shared pool, and the redo log buffer
PMON, SMON, and DBWn
Sort areas and session-specific cursor state
Datafiles, control files, and redo log files
questions.explain: The SGA's major components described in this lesson are the buffer cache, the shared pool, and the redo log buffer — all shared by the whole instance.

questions.q: How does the PGA fundamentally differ from the SGA, per this lesson?
options: The PGA is private, per-server-process memory, while the SGA is shared by every process connected to the instance
The PGA is shared across all sessions, while the SGA is private to one process
The PGA and SGA are two names for the exact same memory region
The PGA only exists in Oracle RAC configurations
questions.explain: Each server process gets its own private PGA (for sort areas, cursor state, etc.), unlike the SGA, which every process shares.
